newsitem.title: POLAND: INTERVIEW-POLISH PZU INSURER MULLS EXPANSION.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-POLISH PZU INSURER MULLS EXPANSION.

text.p: Poland's largest insurance firm Powszechny Zaklad Ubezpieczen SA (PZU), slated for a sell-off in 1997, should become a financial institution providing a wide range of capital market services, its president said on Tuesday.

Jan Monkiewicz said that the state-owned PZU, which has so far dealt with non-life insurance, was considering opening mutual and pension funds, providing asset management and probably para-banking services, possibly next year.
He told Reuters in an interview that his firm's new share issue to selected investors early next year would help launch such products with an injection of capital and expertise.
"We have already started preparations to launch new activities, possibly next year....We are negotiating with leading world and Polish institutions on cooperating in this area," Monkiewicz said.

He said PZU -- which now has only one subsidiary, PZU Zycie life insurer -- could also expand its holding structure, which would enable PZU to cover many types of narrow risks through its daughter companies.

"I do not think PZU should buy typical insurance firms, but I cannot rule out shedding some firms from our structure, purchasing firms or creating new ones -- specialising in one particular risk," he said.

Monkiewicz said that the goals could be achieved if PZU made higher profits and boosted its capital, which currently amounts to 90 million zlotys, and does not meet solvency margin requirements demanded by Polish law.
Last year the firm had a net profit of 105.2 million zlotys on gross premiums of 2.2 billion zlotys. It collected a total of 2.7 billion zlotys in gross premiums in the first three quarters of 1996.
The Polish insurance watchdog has said PZU needed 400 million zlotys to meet the solvency requirements.
Monkiewicz confirmed that PZU hoped to raise some of the funds through the closed issue, which would amount to between 250 and 750 million zlotys.
More capital could come later in 1997, when a public offering is likely to take place, he said.

But Monkiewicz said that the market share of PZU, which controls about 60 percent of Poland's non-life insurance market and 80 percent of the life insurance market through its subsidary, was likely to shrink in the coming years.
He said PZU's position would become weaker because an expected growth of Poland's insurance market would automatically take some market share from PZU.
"I think that in a few years' time PZU's position on the market will be weaker than now, I do not think it will be able to keep its market share, and this is not our strategic goal," Monkiewicz said.
He forecasted that after 1999, when Poland's insurance market is due to completely open up to international competition, PZU's market share would likely fall to about 50 percent.
